pages.text: Five Holmes Cases

image.note: Cover: 221B Baker Street, magnifying glass, fog

pages.text: Contents. The Missing Medal / The Blue Envelope / The Baker's Thumb / The Whistling House / The Vanishing Bicycle.

My name is Doctor Watson, and I share rooms at 221B Baker Street with the cleverest man in London: Mr Sherlock Holmes. What follows are five of the puzzles we solved together. See if you can beat him to the answer.

image.note: 221B sitting room, Holmes and Watson

pages.text: Holmes had a strange and wonderful gift. He could glance at a stranger, at their shoes, their hands, a mark on a sleeve, and tell you where they had been that very morning. "You see, Watson," he would say, "but you do not observe."

image.note: Holmes with a magnifying glass

pages.text: It began with a knock and a boy in a school cap, red-faced and out of breath. "Please, sir," he said, "my swimming medal is gone. It was locked in the class cabinet, and this afternoon the cabinet was still locked, but the medal had vanished."

image.note: Anxious schoolboy at the door

pages.text: "I know who took it," the boy added hotly. "Tom, who sits by the window. He was jealous." Holmes held up a hand. "You suspect Tom. But suspicion is not evidence, and a jealous heart is not a guilty one. Tell me the facts, and leave nothing out, however small."

image.note: Holmes raising a calming hand

pages.text: The medal had sat on the shelf that morning. The window had been open, for the day was warm. No one had a key but the teacher. "Locked," murmured Holmes, "and yet empty. Come, Watson. This is a small puzzle, but a pretty one."

image.note: Holmes reaching for his coat

pages.text: At the school, Holmes did not look at the cabinet first. He looked at the floor beneath the open window, then at the sill, then up at the roof of the building opposite. "Interesting," he said softly. "Very interesting indeed."

image.note: Holmes examining the window sill

pages.text: On the sill lay three things a lesser eye would miss: a scratch in the paint, a single downy feather, and a smear of something white. Holmes touched the smear, and smelled it. "Not a thief in boots," he said, "but a thief on wings."

image.note: Close-up: feather, scratch, white smear

pages.text: "A bird?" I said. "A jackdaw, to be exact," said Holmes. "They are famous thieves, quite mad for anything that shines. It flew in at the open window, took the bright medal from the shelf, and carried it off. And a jackdaw hides its treasure high."

image.note: A jackdaw eyeing something shiny

pages.text: He pointed to the old bell tower across the yard, where the birds wheeled and cawed. "Fetch a ladder, and I believe you will find more than your medal." And so it was. In the untidy nest lay the medal, bright as ever, with two coins, a button, and a shard of mirror.

image.note: Nest full of shiny treasures, medal among them

pages.text: The boy was overjoyed, and ashamed too. "And I blamed Tom." "You did," said Holmes, not unkindly. "Remember this. Everyone looked at the locked door and asked how a person got in. The answer was that no person did. Remove the impossible, Watson, and whatever remains, however unlikely, must be the truth."

image.note: Boy holding the medal, Holmes beside him

pages.text: Our next visitor was a lady in a grey coat, twisting a blue envelope in her gloved hands. "Mr Holmes, for three mornings this has come. No name, no note inside, only this same blue envelope, quite empty. I am frightened. Someone is watching me."

image.note: Worried lady with a blue envelope

pages.text: Holmes took the envelope and turned it to the light. He studied the stamp, the smudged postmark, and the address, written in a shaky, old-fashioned hand. He said nothing for a full minute. Then, to my surprise, he smiled.

image.note: Holmes studying the envelope in lamplight

pages.text: "Tell me," he said gently, "have you an elderly relative? An uncle, perhaps, or a grandfather, who lives alone?" The lady blinked. "My great-uncle Albert. But he is nearly ninety, and forgets his own name half the time."

image.note: The lady surprised by the question

pages.text: "Then here is your watcher," said Holmes kindly. "See the postmark: each was posted from the very village where your great-uncle lives. See the hand: shaky, and old. He addresses the envelope, and forgets to put the letter inside. Three times he has meant to write, and three times forgotten the letter itself."

image.note: Postmark and shaky handwriting, magnified

pages.text: The lady's fear melted into something softer. "Poor Uncle Albert. All alone, trying to reach me." "You should visit him soon," said Holmes. "I suspect he is not frightening you at all. He is missing you." She left with tears in her eyes, but they were not sad ones.

image.note: The lady leaving, moved, clutching the envelope

pages.text: "You see, Watson," Holmes said afterwards, "fear makes people imagine the worst. She saw a spy. I saw a lonely old man and a forgetful hand. The very same envelope, read two ways. Always read the clue, and not the fear."

image.note: Holmes by the fire, thoughtful

pages.text: One morning a large, floury man burst in, wringing his apron. "They say I did it, Mr Holmes! A gold watch gone from the shop beside my bakery, and the constable says I took it, for I was near the window at the very hour. But I am no thief!"

image.note: Distressed baker in a floury apron

pages.text: "Calm yourself. When was the watch taken?" "At ten o'clock, they say." Holmes looked at the man's hands, his arms, and the fine white dust on his sleeves. "And at ten o'clock, what were you doing?" "Kneading the second batch, sir, as I do every single morning."

image.note: Holmes examining the baker's floury hands

pages.text: "To the bakery," said Holmes. There he examined the great bowls, the ovens, and a wooden beam above the kneading table, dusted thick with flour. On the beam, clear as day, were the marks of ten floury fingers, pressed up as a man pushes down hard to knead.

image.note: Floury fingerprints on a beam above the table

pages.text: "Now the shop next door." The stolen watch had sat on a high shelf. Its dusty surface was scuffed by a hand reaching up, and beside it, on the shelf edge, was a mark. But it was clean. No flour. Not a single speck.

image.note: Holmes pointing to a clean mark on a dusty shelf

pages.text: "But he was seen at his window," the constable objected, folding his arms. "Seen, yes," said Holmes. "A man may stand at a window and still be innocent. Here is proof, not a guess. A baker who kneaded at ten leaves flour on all he touches. See his prints in his own bakery."

image.note: Holmes addressing a stubborn constable

pages.text: "Yet the thief who reached this shelf left a clean mark. Flourless hands took that watch. This man's hands were white to the elbow." The constable frowned, then slowly nodded. The baker was free. "You did not prove who did it," I said later. "Not yet. But I proved who did not, and that is where every honest case must begin."

image.note: Relieved baker shaking Holmes's hand

pages.text: "Our house is haunted," said the two children, quite certain, standing side by side. "Every windy night, a whistling comes from the empty upstairs room. Low, then high. Mother says it is the wind. We say it is a ghost."

image.note: Two solemn children reporting

pages.text: Holmes did not laugh, as many grown men would. "A ghost that only whistles when the wind blows," he said thoughtfully, "is a very obedient ghost. Ghosts, in my experience, keep their own hours. Let us go and listen to yours."

image.note: Holmes reaching for his coat again

pages.text: We reached the house at dusk, as the wind rose. Sure enough, from the locked upstairs room came a whistle: low, then climbing high, then low again, in time with each gust. The children clutched each other. I confess the hair rose on my own neck.

image.note: Dark landing, a closed door, wind outside

pages.text: Holmes, however, was already on his knees at the door, then at the window, then at the empty fireplace. He reached up into the chimney, felt about, and drew out, with a look of triumph, an old cracked clay pot that someone had long ago wedged into the flue.

image.note: Holmes reaching into the chimney

pages.text: "Your ghost," he said, holding it up. "When the wind blows across the broken top of this pot, it whistles, exactly as you would whistle across a bottle. Low for a soft gust, high for a strong one. Your ghost is a jar and a draught, nothing more."

image.note: Cracked pot, wind across its broken mouth

pages.text: The children were half disappointed and half delighted. "So there is no ghost?" "There is something better," said Holmes. "There is an answer. A mystery solved is worth ten mysteries feared. Now you may sleep, and the wind may whistle to an empty chimney all it likes."

image.note: Children smiling, relieved, at the window

pages.text: The last case began outside our own door. A telegram boy left his bicycle at the kerb, ran up with a message, and came down to find it gone. "Two minutes!" he wailed. "I was gone two minutes! It has vanished into thin air!"

image.note: Distraught telegram boy at an empty kerb

pages.text: "Nothing vanishes into thin air," said Holmes, already outside and studying the wet street. "It rained an hour ago. The ground still remembers. Show me exactly where the bicycle stood." The boy pointed. Holmes crouched over the tyre marks pressed into the mud.

image.note: Holmes crouched over tyre tracks in the mud

pages.text: "Curious," he said. "Your bicycle stood here. But look: two sets of tracks lead away, side by side, not one. Two bicycles left this spot, wheeled by hand, together. And here, a boot print smaller than yours."

image.note: Two parallel tyre tracks and a small boot print

pages.text: Holmes followed the tracks around the corner to a narrow yard, where a smaller boy stood puzzling over two identical red bicycles. "There you are," said Holmes. "You did not lose your bicycle, my friend. This lad owns its twin, and in his hurry wheeled both away, thinking a friend had left one for him."

image.note: A puzzled smaller boy with two identical bicycles

pages.text: The mix-up was soon sorted, each bicycle to its owner, and no thief in sight. The telegram boy stared. "But how did you know it was not stolen?" "A thief rides away fast, on one bicycle," said Holmes. "He does not walk slowly, wheeling two. The tracks told the whole tale, to anyone who troubled to read them."

image.note: Both boys with their own bikes, sorted

pages.text: As we climbed the stairs, Holmes was smiling. "Five puzzles, Watson, and not a single ghost, spy, or master thief among them. Only the world, being ordinary, and people, forgetting to look. That is the great secret. Observe what is truly there, not what you fear or expect."

image.note: Holmes and Watson climbing the stairs

pages.text: How to think like Holmes. One: observe, do not merely see. Two: notice the small thing everyone else steps over. Three: remove what is impossible, and what remains is your answer. Four: read the clue, not your fear. Five: the ordinary explanation is usually the true one.

image.note: Magnifying glass over the five rules

pages.text: Five cases closed. But London is full of puzzles, and Baker Street is never quiet for long. Keep your eyes open, reader. One day you may spot a clue that even Mr Holmes has missed.

image.note: Foggy Baker Street, a new client approaching
